claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature, single-phase BCC alloy.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between the BCC–FCC Gibbs free-energy difference and kinetic barriers.
The Gibbs free-energy difference between BCC and FCC is a critical parameter for transformations and phase stability in multicomponent alloys.
Sluggish atomic diffusion is a notable kinetic barrier in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Rapid cooling suppresses atomic rearrangement and retains the high-temperature BCC phase despite a possible lower-temperature thermodynamic preference for another phase.
Extended exposure at intermediate temperature permits diffusion-mediated nucleation of FCC when the BCC–FCC free-energy difference favors FCC.
The BCC-to-FCC transformation proceeds through nanoscale nuclei formed at grain boundaries or defects.
Atomic diffusion facilitates the formation and growth of the proposed FCC nuclei.
Slower cooling or annealing allows the alloy to approach the equilibrium phase state dictated by the BCC–FCC Gibbs free-energy difference.
Rapidly quenched samples will largely retain BCC.
Slow-cooled or intermediate-annealed samples will have a larger FCC phase fraction than rapidly quenched samples.
The increase in FCC fraction will be proportional to the predicted reduction in the relevant Gibbs free-energy difference.
The transformed phase fraction can be predicted from calculated free-energy differences together with the time available for diffusion.
The proposed mechanism applies below the high-temperature BCC stabilization range but above temperatures at which atomic mobility is effectively frozen.
Grain size and defect density may alter the transformation kinetics and resulting phase fractions.
A controlled comparison of rapidly quenched and slowly cooled or annealed samples can test the predicted cooling-rate dependence.

Failure of the slow-cooled or annealed samples to show a statistically significant FCC increase, or failure of phase fraction to correlate with predicted free-energy differences, would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls rapidly cooled BCC 'stable,' whereas the mechanism describes it as a kinetically retained metastable high-temperature phase.

Rapid quenching is a central comparison with an explicit prediction, but the boundary statement says extremely rapid cooling may fall outside the hypothesis's predictive scope without defining where that exclusion begins.
